correctness.rationale: Writing L(t)=sigma(t)-t-1, a quasi-amicable pair is exactly a two-cycle of L. A prime maps to zero. A prime square p^2 maps to p and then to zero. If t=pq with distinct primes, L(t)=p+q<t=pq. Hence if both members had Omega at most two, both would be composite semiprimes; the square case is impossible, while two squarefree semiprimes would force m>n and n>m simultaneously. This proves the unrestricted Omega barrier. The packaged finite sweep is only corroborative.
residual_risks: No claim is made about pairs where one member has Omega at least three.

originality.rationale: Hagis-Lord's primary paper proves that relatively prime quasi-amicable pairs have at least four distinct prime factors in the product and separately proves that a prime-power member must have odd exponent greater than three. Those statements do not cover the remaining non-coprime squarefree-semiprime branch. Pollack's full 2011 article studies asymptotic density and does not state a semiprime classification. Current Resultary searches found no prior unrestricted Omega<=2 barrier. Originality therefore passes to the best of current knowledge, with older unindexed observations retained as a risk.

value.rationale: The theorem gives a complete and unrestricted classification of the lowest nontrivial multiplicative-complexity layer for a classical aliquot two-cycle problem. Although the final contradiction is elementary, the boundary is natural and directly complements published low-factor restrictions; this is a motivated structural cutoff rather than an arbitrary exercise.
residual_risks: The barrier is deliberately modest and gives no information once either member has three or more prime factors.
